{{nihongo|'''Miwa Shrine (Higashisue, Setouchi)'''|美和神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Osafune, Okayama|Q7105505|qid=Q7105505}}, {{ill|Setouchi, Okayama|Q691691|qid=Q691691}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|Q132936|qid=Q132936}}. The enshrined deity is {{ill|Ōmononushi|fr|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主|mni|ꯑꯣꯃꯣꯅꯣꯅꯨꯁꯤ|ru|Омононуси|simple|Ōmononushi|zh|大物主|qid=Q10936701|lt=Ōmononushi-no-Mikoto}}. It is a {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=shikinaisha (small shrine)}}. There is another shrine of the same name in Osafune-chō, {{ill|Miwa Shrine (Fukusato, Setouchi)|Q11608849|qid=Q11608849|lt=Miwa Shrine}}. Under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern shrine ranking system}}, its rank was gōsha. {{nihongo|'''Miwa Shrine (Higashisue, Setouchi)'''|美和神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Bizen Province]].

== Overview ==
It stands on Mt. Hirotaka (166{{ill|Metre|Q11573|qid=Q11573|lt=m}}). Since ancient times, Mt. Hirotaka was called Miwa-no-mine and, like {{ill|Mount Miwa|Q860627|qid=Q860627}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|Q131287|qid=Q131287}}, was revered as a sacred mountain. At the mountain’s north foot are {{ill|Tsukiyama Kofun (Setouchi city)|Q11603502|qid=Q11603502|lt=Tsukiyama Kofun}} and the Fudasaki Kofun group; at the south foot is the Sazarashi Kofun group. These {{ill|Kofun|ca|Kofun|cs|Kofun|da|Kofun|de|Kofun|eo|Kofun|es|Kofun|fa|کوفون|fi|Kofun|fr|Kofun|he|קופון (רוגם)|hr|Kofun (grobnica)|it|Kofun|ja|古墳|ko|고훈|my|ခိုဖွန်း|pl|Kofun (kurhan)|pt|Kofun|ru|Кофун (захоронение)|simple|Kofun|th|โคฟุง|tr|Kofun|uk|Кофун|zh|古墳|qid=Q1141225}} show the surrounding area had been inhabited since ancient times.

A legend explains the mountain’s name through Empress {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}’s beloved horse “Shirataka” (White Hawk). While the empress was staying by boat at Kaburazaki in {{ill|Ushimado, Okayama|Q204799|qid=Q204799}}, the horse accidentally fell into the sea. It swam to the north shore, ran up the mountain, and died there. Local people buried it carefully on the mountain. The mountain then came to be called “Shirataka-yama,” which later changed in pronunciation to “Hirotaka-yama.”

At the summit is an {{ill|Iwakura rock|Q11587880|qid=Q11587880}}, called Okutsu Iwakura. After shrine buildings were built, the sacred object was transferred to the honden. Around the iwakura, small stones are laid out in a square, each side 11 meters.

According to shrine tradition, it was divided and invited from {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|Q705542|qid=Q705542}} in {{ill|Sakurai, Nara|Q127026|qid=Q127026}}, Nara Prefecture. The date is unknown. According to the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}} and ''Bizen-koku Shikishakō'', its {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|Q11591025|qid=Q11591025}} was Junior Third Rank; records from {{ill|Ōei|Q1193078|qid=Q1193078}} ({{ill|1394|Q6398|qid=Q6398}}–{{ill|1427|Q6305|qid=Q6305}}) and {{ill|Meiō|Q1193841|qid=Q1193841}} ({{ill|1492|Q6679|qid=Q6679}}–{{ill|1501|Q6131|qid=Q6131}}) list it as Senior Third Rank.

Oral tradition, however, says it was relocated from Hirotaka Shrine in Shirikai, {{ill|Oku, Okayama|Q7082701|qid=Q7082701}}, in the same city<ref>''Oku-gun-shi, Part 2''</ref>. As a remnant of this, during the autumn grand festival, priests and attendants go to Shirikai, perform purification in seawater, and offer sake and rice to Hirotaka Shrine.

In the {{ill|Sengoku period|Q204023|qid=Q204023}}, during {{ill|Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341}} ({{ill|1558|Q6601|qid=Q6601}}–{{ill|1570|Q6659|qid=Q6659}}), lord of {{ill|Kanagawa Castle|Q11647049|qid=Q11647049}} {{ill|Matsuda Mototeru|Q11531997|qid=Q11531997|lt=Matsuda Sakon Shōgen Motokata}} and his son {{ill|Matsuda Motokata|Q11531996|qid=Q11531996|lt=Motokata}}, believers in {{ill|Nichiren-shū|Q206611|qid=Q206611}}, pressed temples and shrines to convert and suppressed those who refused. Because only {{ill|Hachiman|Q261637|qid=Q261637}} was treated as a deity invited by the Lotus teaching, this shrine is said to have escaped destruction by renaming itself Hirotaka Hachimangū. It was called by that name throughout the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}. In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 3 ({{ill|1870|Q7741|qid=Q7741}}), it resumed the name Miwa Shrine; in Meiji 6 ({{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}}) it became gōsha. On January 27, Meiji 40 ({{ill|1907|Q2048|qid=Q2048}}), it was designated a shrine receiving official offerings. On January 11, Meiji 43 ({{ill|1910|Q2075|qid=Q2075}}), it merged Aoki Shrine (village shrine; deity: {{ill|Amaterasu|abstract|Q455602|ar|أماتيراسو|ary|أماطيراسو|az|Amaterasu|bcl|Amaterasu|be|Аматэрасу|be_x_old|Аматэрасу|bew|Amatérasu|bg|Аматерасу|ca|Amaterasu|cs|Amaterasu|da|Amaterasu|de|Amaterasu|el|Αματεράσου|eo|Amaterasu|es|Amaterasu|et|Amaterasu|eu|Amaterasu|fa|آماتراسو|fi|Amaterasu|fr|Amaterasu|gl|Amaterasu|he|אמטראסו|hi|अमातेरसु|hr|Amaterasu|hu|Amateraszu Ómikami|hy|Ամատերասու Օմիկամի|id|Amaterasu|it|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|jv|Amaterasu|ka|ამატერასუ|ko|아마테라스 오미카미|la|Amaterasu|lb|Amaterasu|lt|Amaterasu|lv|Amaterasu|min|Amaterasu|ml|അമതേരസു|mni|ꯑꯃꯇꯦꯔꯁꯨ ꯑꯣꯃꯤꯀꯃꯤ|ms|Amaterasu|nl|Amaterasu|nn|Amaterasu|no|Amaterasu|or|ଆମାତେରାଶୁ|pa|ਆਮਾਤੇਰਸ|pl|Amaterasu|pt|Amaterasu|ro|Amaterasu|rsk|Аматерасу|ru|Аматэрасу|sco|Amaterasu|sh|Amaterasu|simple|Amaterasu Ōmikami|sk|Amaterasu Ómikami|sl|Amaterasu|sr|Аматерасу|su|Amaterasu|sv|Amaterasu|ta|அமதெரசு|th|อามาเตราซุ|tl|Amaterasu|tok|jan sewi suli Amatelasu|tr|Amaterasu|uk|Аматерасу|uz|Amaterasu|vi|Amaterasu|wuu|天照大神|zh|天照大神|zh_min_nan|Amaterasu|zh_yue|天照大神|qid=Q455602}}’s rough spirit).
